claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily governed by formation of a protective chromium oxide layer.
The chromium oxide layer acts as a barrier to corrosive species.
The study steels are initially uncorroded and contain at least 10 wt.% chromium.
The steels will be exposed to a sodium chloride solution at 300°C and 1 atm.
Chromium content, temperature, and exposure time will be varied in the controlled study.
Corrosive exposure causes formation of a chromium oxide layer.
The chromium oxide layer reduces diffusion of corrosive species to the steel surface.
Steels containing at least 10 wt.% chromium will exhibit a 50% lower corrosion rate than a baseline steel containing 5 wt.% chromium under the same exposure conditions.
Corrosion rate will be assessed using weight loss and surface analysis.
The proposed mechanism should hold for chromium contents of 10–20 wt.%, temperatures of 200–400°C, and exposure times up to 1000 hours.
The exact process of chromium oxide formation and its relationship to corrosion resistance is not fully understood.
Grain size and impurities may influence the corrosion behavior.
Failure to reduce corrosion rate by at least 30% relative to the 5 wt.% chromium baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe formation of a chromium oxide layer would falsify the hypothesis.
